# Foreword

This operating model is for conducting are exploratory, didactic analyses and is not intended to inform management decision making at this stage. All data used in the construction of these operating models are publicly available from sources that are cited. 

<br>
<hr>


# Introduction

This operating model (OM) aims to closely mimic a recent reference set of OMs for shallow-water Cape hake, *Merluccius capensis*, by [Ross-Gillespie et al. (2025)](https://zivahub.uct.ac.za/articles/standard/Update_to_the_hake_Reference_Case_Operating_Model_with_inclusion_of_the_2024_commercial_data/30680402/1), for the purposes of testing the robustness of management procedures to projected climate changes originating from an Atlantis Ecosystem Model ([Ortega-Cisneros et al. 2018][https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/fog.12268]). 

*M. capensis* is caught off the south and west coasts of South Africa together with the deep-water Cape hake, *M. paradoxus*. The two species are hard to distinguish. Catches are split between them using a species-splitting algorithm (Ross-Gillespie and Butterworth, 2024). Most of the *M. capensis* catch comes from the offshore trawl fleet on both coasts. The remaining catch is taken by the inshore trawl fleet on the south coast, by longline on both coasts and by a south-coast handline fishery. The handline fishery was significant in the early 2000s (up to 7.3 thousand tons in 2001) but has been much reduced since around 2010. Total *M. capensis* catches peaked at about 53 thousand tons in 1985 and have since fluctuated between about 20 and 39 thousand tons, averaging about 28 thousand tons over 2014–2023 (22.5 thousand tons in 2023). 

The resource is managed under OMP-2022, a management procedure tested against a Reference Set of nine age-structured, species- and sex-disaggregated operating models. These models are conditioned on commercial catches, GLM-standardised CPUE series, research survey abundance estimates (west coast summer and south coast autumn series from 1985 and 1988 respectively) and catch-at-length and age–length data. The Reference Set spans three stock–recruitment forms (Ricker, and Beverton–Holt with steepness of 0.9 or 0.7) and three central years for the assumed historical catch series (1952, 1958 and 1963). In the 2024 update, the Reference Case model (Ricker, central year 1958) estimates female spawning biomass of 175 thousand tons in 2024. That is 77% of the pristine level and about three times B_MSY. Most of the other Reference Set models also estimate the stock to be well above B_MSY. However, two runs estimate a much more depleted *M. capensis stock*, and the authors note that the data do not determine depletion well (Ross-Gillespie and Butterworth, 2024). The 2025 update of the Reference Case adds the 2024 commercial data (Ross-Gillespie et al., 2025).

The focus of this operating model is capturing the overall stock dynamics in terms of resilience, magnitude and natural variability for the purpose of evaluating under projection, various management porcedures (MP) that set annual advice. As such the focus here is not capturing the detailed historical spatial and seasonal dynamics necessary to interpret historical data correctly (a primary challenge for the assessment) but rather to use the assessment estimates for evaluating MPs. For this reason the operating model is sex aggregated (somatic growth and weight at length, is very similar among male and female hake in any case). In this Climate Test application we chose to use the Ricker stock-recruitment assumption of Ross-Gillepsie and Butterworth (2024) since it provides greater contrast in historical biomass levels and a higher sensitivity to possible climate impacts on stock productivity. The historical catch series used for conditioning was relatively non-impactful and the central '1958' series was used for OM construction in this application.

# Methods

## Data Extraction from Conditioned Operating models

Catch data, survey data, growth estimates, weight at length relationships and model estimates of biomass and stock status were digitally extracted from the operating model conditioning reports of Rademeyer et al. (2019), Ross-Gillepsie and Butterworth (2024) and Ross-Gillespie et al. (2025):

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
library(readxl)

setwd("C:/GitHub/ClimateTestMethods/docs/OMs/Hake")
xlsx <- "data/M_capensis_hake_extract.xlsx"   # edit path as needed

rd <- function(sheet, range, names) {
  df <- as.data.frame(read_excel(xlsx, sheet = sheet, range = range,
                                 col_names = names, na = c("", "-")))
  df[rowSums(!is.na(df)) > 0, , drop = FALSE]   # drop any fully empty rows
}

# 1. M. capensis catches by fleet (thousand t), Table 1, 1978-2023
#    Blank in source ("-") -> NA. Total columns are the workbook formulas' values.
catches <- rd("Catches_Mcapensis", "A5:J50",
  c("Year", "Offshore_WC", "Offshore_SC", "Inshore_SC", "Longline_WC",
    "Longline_SC", "Handline_SC", "Offshore_total", "Longline_total", "All_total"))

# 2. M. capensis survey biomass and s.e. (thousand t), Table 3b, 1985-2024
survey <- rd("Survey_Mcapensis", "A5:I44",
  c("Year", "WC_Summer", "WC_Summer_se", "WC_Winter", "WC_Winter_se",
    "SC_Spring", "SC_Spring_se", "SC_Autumn", "SC_Autumn_se"))

# 3. Figure 2a panels 11/14/17 (RS02, Ricker, central year 1958), digitized, 1917-2024
#    Bsp_K is NA for 1917-1925 (line hidden behind the panel label).
fig2a <- rd("Fig2a_RS02_digitized", "A5:D112",
  c("Year", "Bsp", "Bsp_K", "Bsp_BMSY"))

#    Cross-check of digitized values against Table 4b
fig2a_check <- rd("Fig2a_RS02_digitized", "A116:D120",
  c("Quantity", "Table4b", "Digitized", "Difference"))

# 4. Figure B.9 M. capensis female length-at-age (RS03 orange curve), digitized
growth_int  <- rd("FigB9_growth_Mcap_F", "A5:B20",  c("Age", "Length_cm"))   # ages 0-15
growth_grid <- rd("FigB9_growth_Mcap_F", "D5:E155", c("Age", "Length_cm"))   # 0.1-yr grid

# 5. Length-weight parameters, W(g) = alpha * L(cm)^beta (2019 RC spec, Table 7)
lw_params <- rd("LengthWeight", "A5:D8", c("Species", "Sex", "alpha", "beta"))

#    Weight-at-age for M. capensis females from the Figure B.9 lengths
weight_at_age <- rd("LengthWeight", "A13:D28",
  c("Age", "Length_cm", "Weight_g", "Weight_kg"))

# Quick checks
str(catches); str(survey); str(fig2a); str(growth_int); str(lw_params)

# Example: convert any length (cm) to weight (g) for M. capensis females
p <- subset(lw_params, Species == "M. capensis" & Sex == "Female")
len2wt <- function(L) p$alpha * L^p$beta
len2wt(c(30, 50, 70))

```


## OpenMSE 2.0

OpenMSE operating models were configured to match the aggregate age-structured dynamics of the [stock assessment](https://science.uct.ac.za/sites/default/files/media/documents/science_uct_ac_za/2066/iws-2025-sardine-bg4.pdf) closely matching the estimates of harvest rate, recruitment and biomass. 

## OM Initialization 

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
library(openMSE)
library(readxl)
packageVersion('MSEtool') # should be v4x

# AI extracted estimates of recent assessed biomass, recruitment, harvest rate, selectivity, maturity and somatic growth
est_yr =  as.data.frame(readxl::read_xlsx('Data/SA_Sardine_2025_estimates.xlsx', 'ByYear'))
est_len = as.data.frame(readxl::read_xlsx('Data/SA_Sardine_2025_estimates.xlsx', 'ByLength'))
est_age = as.data.frame(readxl::read_xlsx('Data/SA_Sardine_2025_estimates.xlsx', 'ByAge'))

# Create blank operating model and fill details
om = new('om') 
om@Name = "South African Sardine"
om@Longitude = 20
om@Latitude  = -35
om@Author = 'Tom Carruthers'
om@Agency = 'Blue Matter'
om@Email = 'tom@bluematterscience.com'
om@Region = "South Africa"
om@Sponsor = "The Ocean Foundation"
om@Source = "https://climatetest.bluematterscience.com"

# Basic Config
Years = est_yr$Year           # historical year labels
ny = length(Years)            # number of historical years
om@nYear = ny                 # historical year
om@pYear = 50                 # 50 projected years
om@Interval = 1               # management updated every 1 year
om@DataLag = 1                # data available from last year (not in-season management)
om@nSim = 48                  # No. realisations of stock and fleet dynamics
om@CurrentYear = max(Years)   # label for most recent historical year
om@Years = Years(om)          # all year labels
om@Seasons = 1                # Annual OM
om@maxF = 3                   # maximum apical exploitation rate is 3.0 (harvest rate of 95%)
om@Seed = 1                   # random seed for stochastic sampling
om@Log[[1]] = paste("OM created:", Sys.Date()) 

```

## Stock and Fleet Initialization 

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
stock = new('stock')
stock@Name = 'South African Sardine'
stock@CommonName = 'Sardine'
stock@Species = 'Sardinops sagax'

fleet = new('fleet')
fleet@Name = "All commercial fleets (inc directed sardine and round herring)"
```


## Natural mortality rate 

The operating model assumes the same natural mortality as the recent stock assessment (following the 2022 assessment of [de Moor (2022)](https://doi.org/10.25375/uct.22146602.v1)) that is 1.0 per year for juveniles (age 0) and 0.8 for mature fish (age 1+). The recruitment outputs we are conditioning on are end of age-0 and subject to the initial year of mortality, hence we assume zero mortality for age class zero in the OM. 

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
stock@Ages = Ages(6, MinAge = 0)                                            # Age 6 is the last age class for calculations of age-based vectors
stock@NaturalMortality = NaturalMortality(MeanAtAge = c(0, rep(0.8, 6)))   
plot(stock@Ages@Classes,stock@NaturalMortality@MeanAtAge, pch=19, lwd=2, xlab = "Age", ylim = c(0,1), ylab = "Inst. Nat. M. (per year)"); grid()
```

## Somatic Growth

The operating model assumes an length-at-age vector that is the unweighted mean of the South and West curves used by the 2025 assessment [de Moor 2025](https://science.uct.ac.za/sites/default/files/media/documents/science_uct_ac_za/2066/iws-2025-sardine-bg4.pdf).

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
Classes = 1:ceiling(max(est_age$Length)*1.3)   
stock@Length = Length(MeanAtAge = c(est_age$Length,est_age$Length[6]),  # Need to add another asympotic length to make 7 age classes (first is age-0)
                      Classes = 1:ceiling(max(est_age$Length)*1.3) )    # Length classes
plot(0:6,stock@Length@MeanAtAge, lwd=2, type="l",xlab = "Age", ylab = "Length (cm)"); grid()
```

## Weight-at-Length

The weight length-weight relationship follows that derived by [OLSPS Marine](refs/FISHERIES_2023_NOV_SWG-PEL_24Rev Sardine W-L Further Regressions.pdf). The relationship for both stock units combined is assumed to follow the relationship: 

W = 0.0000071118 * L ^ 3.181             (cm - kg)

Note that if MP advice is unitless (e.g. catch in the projection relative to catch in 2024) the length-weight relationship is largely inconsequential. To obtain the same scale the length-weight relationship is exactly inversly related to unfished recruitment and numbers are not used in the model. 

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, fig.width= 7}
LT =  stock@Length@MeanAtAge 
WT =  0.0000071118 * LT ^ 3.181
stock@Weight = Weight(MeanAtAge = WT)

par(mfrow=c(1,2),mai=c(0.9,0.9,0.6,0.05))
plot(0:6, WT, xlab="Age",ylab = "Weight (kg)",type="l", lwd=1.5)
plot(LT, WT, type="l",lwd=1.5,xlab="Length (cm)",ylab = "Weight (kg)")

```

## Maturity

The maturity ogive followed that specified by a preliminary MSE operating model of [de Moor (2025)](https://science.uct.ac.za/sites/default/files/media/documents/science_uct_ac_za/2066/iws-2025-sardine-bg5.pdf). This prescribes a logistic model with a length 50% maturity of 11.8811 cm with a rate of increase in maturity at length of 1.9311

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
stock@Maturity = Maturity(MeanAtLength = 1/(1+exp(-(Classes - 11.88)/1.93)), Classes = Classes)
plot(Classes,stock@Maturity@MeanAtLength, lwd=2, type="l",xlab = "Length (cm)", ylab = "Fraction Mature"); grid()
```

## Recruitment

Annual recruitment estimates for the West and South stock components were summed to obtain overall stock recruitment. This was related to estimated biomass to derive two model parameters: unfished recruitment (R0, scale, carring capacity) and steepness (resilience). 

This analysis should be derived from the estimates of spawning stock biomass (SSB) from the stock assessment but these are not provided in the publically available reports. 

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}

B = est_yr$B_west + est_yr$B_south # Biomass Mt (could be unitless, R0 and steepness h are the targets)
R = (est_yr$R_west + est_yr$R_south) # Billions of fish (technically, rec observations are June and need inflated by age 0 M)

BH<-function(par, B, R, mode='opt', plot = F, tplot = F, curyr = 2024, pmu = 0.6, pcv = 0.1){ # optimization function for Bev-Holt SR
  h = 0.2 + 0.8 * (1 / (1 + exp(par[1]))); R0 = exp(par[2]);  BpR = max(B,na.rm=T) / R0       # logit between 0.2 and 1
  Rpred<-((0.8 * R0 * h * B) / (0.2 * BpR * R0 * (1 - h) + (h - 0.2) * B))                    # predicted recruitment 
  if(plot) {plot(B,R,pch=19); points(B, Rpred,col='red');                                     # plot fitted SR curve 
            legend('topleft',legend=c(paste("h =",round(h,3)),paste("R0 =",round(R0,3))),text.col="red",bty="n")}
  if(mode=='opt')return(-sum(dnorm(log(Rpred)-log(R),0,0.5,log=T), na.rm=T)-dnorm(pmu,h,pcv,log=T))  # add prior on h
  if(mode != "opt") return(log(R / Rpred))                                                    # return log rec devs
}

opt = optim(par = c(0,log(max(R,na.rm=T)/2)), BH, # optimize for h and R0 from initial values of 0.6 and half the max R
            B =  B, R = R, method = "L-BFGS-B",   # bounded optimization
            lower = c(-4,log(10)),                # broad limits
            upper = c(4,log(50)))                 # broad limits


RD = BH(opt$par, B, R, plot=T, mode = "devs") # recruitment deviations  
R0 = exp(opt$par[2]) * 1E9                    # 'unfished' recruitment
h = 0.2 + 0.8 * (1 / (1 + exp(opt$par[1])))   # steepness of the B-H S-R function
AC = acf(RD[!is.na(RD)],1)$acf[2,1,1]         # lag-1 recruitment autocorrelation
SD = sd(RD, na.rm=T)                          # lognormal recruitment process error ('sigma-R')          


DepGuess = (B[1]/quantile(B,0.5,na.rm=T))                                   # depletion guess
RecDevInit = matrix(DepGuess, nrow = om@nSim, ncol = stock@Ages@MaxAge)     # initial rec devs go into year 1 of RecDevHist
RecDevHist = matrix(exp(RD),nrow = om@nSim, ncol = ny, byrow = T)           # historical rec devs
RecDevProj = matrix(NA,nrow = om@nSim, ncol = om@pYear)                     # projected rec devs
nterminal = sum(is.na(RD))                                                  # No. terminal years in need of filling
fyears = rev(rev(om@Years)[1:(nterminal + om@pYear)])                       # labels for years that need filling
res = MSEtool::GenResiduals(SD, rep(AC,om@nSim), fyears, om@nSim, TruncSD = 3, 
                            LastError = exp(RecDevHist[,ny-nterminal]))     # generated residuals with AC and SD
RecDevHist[,(ny-nterminal+1):ny] = res[,1:nterminal]                        # populate terminal rec devs
RecDevProj = res[, (nterminal+1):ncol(res)]                                 # populate projected rec devs

stock@SRR = SRR(Pars=list(h=h), R0 = R0, AC = AC, RecDevInit = RecDevInit,  # build Stock Rec. Rel. slot
                RecDevHist = RecDevHist, RecDevProj = RecDevProj)

matplot(Years(om, Period = "P"), t(RecDevProj[1:4,]),lty=1,type="l",
        xlab="Proj. Year",ylab ="Rec. Dev.", main="4 Simulations"); grid()
legend('topleft',legend=c(paste("SD =",round(SD,2)),paste("Lag-1 AC =", round(AC,2))))

```

The estimated stock biomass and estimated recruitment cannot be considered as independent (biomass) and dependent (recruitment) variables because biomass itself is a product of recruitment, and this is particularly the case for short-lived species such as sardine. The inter-dependency of these variables generally leads to an overestimate of stock resilience because higher than average recruitment is required at low stock sizes (and vice versa) to drive changes in the biomass levels. 

It is therefore remarkable how little recruitment compensation is estimated (even in this post-hoc fitting). In this case, a relatively informative prior on a steepness (a level of 0.6 which is moderate resilience) barely drags steepness estimates above a value of 0.3. Without this prior, the estimated steepness tends to its lowest possible value of 0.2 which is ecologically implausible (a stock without compensation has a very high probability of extinction). 

This analysis should be revised and updated given SSB estimates from the assessment. 


## Selectivity 

Commercial fishery selectivity follows the length-based-vector of the most recent estimated year of the stock assessment. 

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}

nl = length(Classes)                                        # No. length classes
MeanAtLength = rep(0, nl)                                   # fill a vector with zero selectivity
ind = match(est_len$Length, Classes)                        # get correct indexing for estimated selectivity
MeanAtLength[ind] = est_len$Selectivity                     # map estimated selectivity
MeanAtLength[max(ind):nl] = 1                               # fill upper range with 100% selectivity (asymptotic)

fleet@Selectivity = Selectivity(MeanAtLength = MeanAtLength,
                                Classes = Classes)

plot(Classes,MeanAtLength, lwd=2, type="l",xlab = "Length (cm)", ylab = "Commercial Selectivity", main = "Estimated by Assessment in 2024"); grid()
lines(Classes,stock@Maturity@MeanAtLength, lwd=1.5, lty=2,col='red'); 
legend('topleft', legend = c("Selectivity", "Fraction Mature"),text.col = c("black","red"),bty='n')

```

## Apical F

The stock assessment reports provide a time-series estimate of harvest rate (U) for the combined West and South components. This is converted to an guess of apical F that will be later adjusted to match historical biomass estimates. 


```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}

U = est_yr$U                                              # harvest rate times series (S and W combined)
Adj_vuln = 0.5                                            # apical F and selectivity curve is 50% of the biomass available (U)
F_guess = -log(1-U) / Adj_vuln                            # initial guess of F time series
Eff = matrix(F_guess, nrow=om@nSim, ncol=ny, byrow = T, 
             dimnames = list(1:om@nSim,Years(om,'h')))    # Effort matrix with correct year labels
fleet@Effort = Effort(Effort = Eff)                       # Populate historical effort slot
fleet@Catchability = Catchability(Efficiency = 1)         # Populate catchability slot, F = qE, hence F = E as specified

```


## Initial OM

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
om@Stock = stock
om@Fleet = fleet
hist = Simulate(om)
```



## Scale optimization

Two components of the OM specification need to be adjusted to match estimated biomass, recruitment and harvest rate: unfished recruitment (scale), apical F mismatch. 

To do this we initialize the OM, estimate harvest rate, biomass and recruitment and wrap this into a bivariate optimization for unfished recruitement and apical F modifiers. 

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, message = FALSE, fig.width = 7.5}
ctrl = SimControl(DynamicUnfished = FALSE,
                     RefLandings = FALSE,
                     RefRemovals = FALSE,
                     ConditionObs = FALSE,
                     EstimateBeta = FALSE,
                     GenerateData = FALSE,
                     MSYRefs = FALSE,
                     RefPoints = FALSE,
                     MGT = FALSE,
                     BLow = FALSE)


Apply_pars = function(om, pars){
  R0mult = exp(pars[1])
  Emult = exp(-pars[1]) * exp(pars[2])                      # fried egg please!
  om@Stock@SRR@R0 = om@Stock@SRR@R0 * R0mult
  om@Fleet@Effort@Effort =  om@Fleet@Effort@Effort * Emult
  om
}


doplot = function(om, B, R, Best, Rest, pars, obj){
  par(mfrow =c(1,2),mai=c(0.5,0.9,0.2,0.05))
  ind = !is.na(R); yrs = Years(om, 'h')[ind]
  matplot(yrs, cbind(R[ind],Rest[ind]), ylab = "Recruitment (B)", col=c("black","red"),lty=1,lwd=1.5,type = 'l');grid()
  legend('topleft',legend=c("Assessment","OpenMSE"),text.col = c("black","red"), bty="n")
  matplot(yrs,cbind(B[ind],Best[ind]),ylab="Biomass (Mt)", col=c("black","red"),lty=1,lwd=1.5,type = 'l');grid()
  legend('topleft',legend=c(paste("R0 multiplier =",round(exp(pars[1]),3)),
                            paste("Effort multiplier =",round(exp(-pars[1]) * exp(pars[2]),3)),
                            paste("Obj. F. =", round(obj,5))), text.col = "red", bty="n")
}  

plotstat = function(om2, B, R, ctrl, opt){
  hist = Simulate(om2, control=ctrl)
  Best = hist@Biomass[1,1,] * 1E-9
  Rest = hist@Number[[1]][1,1,,1] * 1E-9
  doplot(om = om2, B, R, Best, Rest, pars = opt$par, obj = opt$value)

}

Int_Scale = function(pars, om, B, R, mode = 'opt', ctrl, plot=F){
  om = Apply_pars(om, pars)
  hist = Simulate(om, control = ctrl)
  Best = hist@Biomass[1,1,] * 1E-9
  Rest = hist@Number[[1]][1,1,,1] * 1E-9
  if(mode == 'opt')  obj = sum(abs(log(Best)-log(B)),na.rm=T) + sum(abs(log(Rest)-log(R)),na.rm=T)
  if(mode == 'optB')  obj = sum(abs(log(Best)-log(B)),na.rm=T)
  if(plot) doplot(om, B, R, Best, Rest, pars, obj)
  if(grepl("opt", mode)){
    return(obj)
  }else{
    pars
  }
} 

opt = optim(c(0,0), Int_Scale, 
      om = om, B = B, R = R, ctrl = ctrl, plot=F,
      method = "L-BFGS-B", control = list(factr = 1E12),
      lower = c(-2, -2), upper = c(2, 2))

om2 = Apply_pars(om,opt$par)
plotstat(om2, B, R, ctrl, opt)


for(i in 1:3){
  hist = Simulate(om2, control=ctrl)
  Best = hist@Biomass[1,1,] * 1E-9
  Rest = hist@Number[[1]][1,1,,1] * 1E-9
  #doplot(om2, B, R, Best, Rest, opt$par, obj = 0)
  ratio = matrix(R/Rest,byrow=T,nrow=om@nSim,ncol=om@nYear)
  ratio[is.na(ratio)] = 1
  R0_adj = exp(log(ratio)*0.5)
  om2@Stock@SRR@RecDevHist[] = om2@Stock@SRR@RecDevHist[] * R0_adj
}

plotstat(om2, B, R, ctrl, opt)

opt2 = optim(c(0,0), Int_Scale, 
            om = om2, B = B, R = R, ctrl = ctrl, mode = "optB", plot=F,
            method = "L-BFGS-B", control = list(factr = 1E12),
            lower = c(-1, -1), upper = c(1, 1))


om3 = Apply_pars(om2,opt2$par)

plotstat(om3, B, R, ctrl, opt2)


```


## Add Generic Observation Model for MP Testing

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}

ExampleObs <- Obs(CPUE = IndicesObs(CV = 0.3),                                # CPUE index
                  Survey = IndicesObs(CV = 0.2, Selectivity = 'SBiomass'),    # spawning biomass survey
                  Landings = CatchObs(CV = 0.025))                            # catches

Obs(om3) <- list(list(ExampleObs))                                            # assign observation error model

hist <- Simulate(om3)                                                         # historical reconstruction
PlotIndexFit(hist, 'CPUE')                                                    # plot historical CPUE 
PlotIndexFit(hist, 'Survey')                                                  # plot historical survey

# Save outputs to the ClimateTest R package for lazyload
SAS = om3
save(SAS, file = "C:/GitHub/ClimateTest/data/SAS.rda")

```



# Results

## Assessment Comparison

The assessment model of de Moor (2025) includes spatial stock components, movement among areas and varying somatic growth and recruitment among areas. This complexity is required to correctly interpret input data to that model. 

However, the aggregate stock-wide recruitment, exploitation rate and abundance is well approximated by the annual, spatially aggregated model applied here. This approximation is suitable for the purposes of this operating model, namely to comparatively rate climate robustness of potential management procedures. 

## Example Projections


```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, fig.width = 7.5}
Hist = Simulate(om3)
MPs = c("CurrentEffort","refMSY","refMSY50","NoFishing")
Proj = Project(Hist, MPs)
muC = apply(Proj@Landings,c(3,5),mean)
muB = apply(Proj@Biomass,c(3,4),mean)
mpcols = c("black","green","blue","red")
yrs = Years(om3, 'p')
par(mfrow =c(1,2),mai=c(0.5,0.9,0.2,0.05))
matplot(yrs, muC/1E6,type="l",lty=1, lwd=1.5, ylab="Mean projected catch (Kt)", col = mpcols)
matplot(yrs, muB/1E6,type="l",lty=1, ylim = c(0, max(muB)*1.05/1E6), lwd=1.5, ylab="Mean projected biomass (Kt)", col = mpcols); grid()
legend('topright', legend=MPs, text.col=mpcols, bty="n")
```

# Software

## OpenMSE

The [openMSE R package](https://openmse.com) was used to organize fishery data, define operating models, condition operating models to data, calculate reference points and specify and test existing and alternative management options. 

Visit the [OpenMSE website](https://openmse.com) for more information on the framework including tutorial and case studies.

The Rapid Conditioning Model is also [described there](https://openmse.com/tutorial-rcm)

Other useful openMSE apps include [MERA](https://www.merafish.org/) for rapidly scoping operating models and [Reference Point Calculator](https://shiny.bluematterscience.com/app/rpc) for investigating reference points and control rules. 

## Climate Test

The Climate Test is an extension of OpenMSE that allows for comparative robustness evaluation of candidate management procedures. For more information please visit the [project splash page](https://climatetest.bluematterscience.com)

## Management Strategy Evaluation

The Ocean Foundation host the [Harvest Strategies website](https://harveststrategies.org/) which is an excellent resource describing MSE, MSE concepts and how MSE can be used in fishery management including introductory videos and interviews with experts. 'Harvest strategy' and Management Procedure are synonymous by the way.
